sections.title: The Challenge
points: Writes must update durable state, indexes, replication, and sometimes shared invariants.
Scaling is constrained by the hottest serialized resource, not merely the total number of application servers.

sections.title: 1) Vertical scaling and write optimization
points: Improve CPU, memory, storage, and transaction efficiency before introducing unnecessary distribution.
Remove unused indexes, shorten transactions, reuse connections, and batch related writes where semantics permit.
B-tree and log-structured storage engines have different read, write, compaction, and space tradeoffs.
A database choice must match access patterns and durability needs rather than a generic SQL-versus-NoSQL slogan.

sections.title: 2) Sharding and partitioning
points: Horizontal sharding distributes records across independent write owners.
Choose a high-cardinality key that spreads traffic and keeps commonly related operations local.
Time-only keys can make the newest partition hot; tenant-only keys can overload a single large tenant.
Vertical partitioning separates data or services with different update patterns, reducing interference.
Cross-shard operations need coordination or redesigned boundaries; sharding does not preserve every single-node convenience.

sections.title: 3) Queues and load shedding
points: A durable queue absorbs short bursts and allows workers to process at a sustainable rate.
Queues do not fix a permanently insufficient processing rate; backlog age grows without bound unless capacity or admission changes.
Return acceptance separately from completion when writes become asynchronous.
Reject, defer, or deprioritize work before overload exhausts memory and causes broader failure.

sections.title: 4) Batching and aggregation
points: Combine many small writes into fewer database operations to amortize network and transaction overhead.
Batch in clients, intermediate processors, or the database interface according to latency and failure requirements.
For counters or metrics, aggregate partial values locally and merge them hierarchically.
Preserve ordering and idempotency where required; retrying a batch must not add the same increments twice.
Larger batches improve throughput but increase delay and the amount of work replayed after failure.

sections.title: When to Use
points: Apply this pattern to event ingestion, telemetry, click aggregation, feed fanout, and other write-heavy pipelines.
First estimate sustained and burst rates and identify whether the limit is storage I/O, lock contention, CPU, or a hot key.
Do not add sharding when a better index, shorter transaction, or modest hardware change solves the actual problem.

sections.title: 1) Resharding
points: Introduce a routing version, copy existing data, and capture concurrent changes during migration.
Switch ownership carefully and retain a rollback or reconciliation path.
Consistent hashing reduces key movement but does not by itself implement safe data transfer or concurrent-write handling.

sections.title: 2) Hot keys
points: More shards do not divide writes to one atomic key.
Split aggregatable counters into subkeys and merge on read or in a second aggregation stage.
Dynamic splitting limits overhead to hot keys but requires routing metadata and a safe merge/transition protocol.
Some invariants cannot be freely split, such as claiming one unique seat; admission control or a serialized owner remains necessary.

sections.title: Conclusion
points: Optimize each write, distribute independent work, smooth bursts, and aggregate where the operation allows it.
Monitor queue age, per-partition load, retries, and compaction or replication lag rather than only total throughput.
Make the consistency and latency cost of each scaling step explicit.
